answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: In ClaimsCore, our claims-adjudication service, I once had a transaction that updated a claim's status and then, inside the same @Transactional method, called out to a notification service to email the policyholder. During our nightly batch settlement run, when a few thousand claims move status at once, that external call held the transaction open long enough that other threads updating the same claims table piled up -- I saw over 90 threads blocked on row locks in one run, which pushed batch runtime from 40 minutes to almost two hours. I moved the notification call out of the transaction entirely: the status update commits on its own, and I write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction, which a separate poller picks up to send the email. Batch runtime dropped back under 45 minutes. The failure I didn't foresee at first: the poller could double-send an email if it crashed after sending but before marking the outbox row done, so I added a sent_at check before resending.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: In ClaimsCore, claim payment submissions to our payment processor carry an idempotency key built from claim_id plus a payment attempt sequence number, stored with a unique constraint in a payment_attempts table. About two years ago, a processor-side timeout caused our retry logic to resend a batch of 60 payment requests with a bug in how the sequence number incremented, so 60 requests reused a sequence number that had already succeeded, and our unique constraint silently rejected the retries as duplicates -- which sounds safe, except six of those claims had genuinely different amounts because of a same-day adjustment, and the retries got dropped instead of processed. I found it during weekly reconciliation when six claims showed as paid in our system but the processor showed no matching transaction. I corrected those six manually with new payment entries, not edits to the rejected ones, and fixed the sequence-number bug so it's tied to payment content, not just an incrementing counter.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I don't have production Rust experience. What I have is a couple of personal projects -- the more serious one is a small tool that ingests our claims export CSVs and cross-checks totals, which I rewrote in Rust over a few weekends to force myself past tutorials. I hit real ownership and lifetime problems doing that, which I can go into detail on. My honest view on migrating something like ClaimsCore: I wouldn't propose a full-service rewrite, I'd want to find one boundary that's stateless and easy to verify by comparing outputs against the existing Java path, run both for a while, and only trust the new one once the outputs matched for a sustained period. That's closer to how I'd want to treat any Rust adoption here, given I'm still building real experience rather than claiming production depth I don't have.
answers.says: If they have production Rust experience, they describe which part of production it was (e.g., why latency became an issue, how they cut the boundary with Java, the measurement results), with numbers and time frames, and can describe failures too. If they lack production experience, they explain the concrete differences from Java in ownership, lifetimes, and async runtimes in their own words, and describe a realistic learning plan (what they have already written, read, or been studying). In addition, they state a view that fits our approach — deciding a boundary and migrating while measuring, rather than a full rewrite — together with their own grounds for it.

answers.text: In Rust code you've actually written — production or a personal project, either is fine — tell me a spot where you got stuck on ownership, lifetimes, or async, and how you resolved it. If you haven't written any yet, just say so.
answers.answer: In my claims-CSV tool, I got stuck trying to hold a reference to the current row while also building up a Vec of parsed rows to return, and the compiler kept rejecting it because the row reference borrowed from the file reader while I was also trying to own the parsed data long-term. I fixed it by having the parse function return owned String and f64 values immediately instead of holding onto references into the reader's buffer, accepting a small amount of copying I'd been trying to avoid. Separately, I fought a Send issue when I tried to share a running total across a couple of threads using a plain Rc, and switched to an Arc<Mutex<_>> once I understood Rc wasn't thread-safe, which felt obvious in hindsight but took me a confused evening to work out.
answers.says: Names concretely what failed to compile in their own code (e.g., a borrow conflict, a lifetime annotation, a Send/Sync constraint, a tokio runtime boundary), how they fixed it, and how they came to understand the fix, in their own words. If it was production work, which part of production it was comes out concretely; if personal, what they built comes out concretely.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: For a ledger-like write path I don't have a production example, but for my claims-CSV tool I did have to decide a boundary of sorts: I kept CSV parsing and validation in Rust, since that's where the tool spends most of its time and where compiler-checked correctness helps most, but I left the eventual write into our reporting database as a separate Python script I already trusted, rather than pulling database access into the Rust side too. What I'd watch in a real production boundary: latency and error rate on the new path, and a running count of any output mismatches against the old path -- the same comparison approach I used to convince myself my Rust totals matched what the old spreadsheet-based process produced before I trusted it.
answers.says: Can describe a general direction for migration, but it stays at generalities (‘measurement matters first,’ ‘migrate in stages’), without describing the concrete boundary location, the metrics to watch, or the decision criteria in their own words. Even when citing past experience carving out a boundary, they can't distinguish what they decided from ‘what the team did,’ and no numbers or failures come up.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: On the same service, we had connection pool exhaustion during month-end reinsurance reporting, when a reporting job ran alongside normal traffic. HikariCP wait time spiked to about 800ms at p95, and normal claim submissions started timing out. I pulled thread dumps during the next occurrence and found the reporting job was holding connections open for the full length of a multi-minute aggregation query instead of releasing them between steps. I rewrote the job to commit and release its connection after each chunk of about 5,000 claims instead of holding one connection for the whole run, and moved it onto a separate 8-connection pool so it couldn't compete with live traffic at all. p95 wait time on the main pool dropped back under 20ms during the next month-end run.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: Around the same period, we had an incident where our adjudication engine's state machine let a claim move from 'approved' straight to 'paid' without passing through a required fraud-review step, for about 45 minutes before I caught it via a mismatch alert on our review-queue depth. Four claims went through that path, totaling around $31,000. I flagged it in our incident channel within ten minutes of noticing, before I'd even confirmed the root cause, paused the affected transition, and had a fix -- a missing state-guard condition -- deployed within two hours. All four claims went through manual fraud review after the fact, and none were found fraudulent, but we still treated it as the process failure it was. The postmortem added an automated test that asserts every terminal state transition passes through its required guard, and I wrote that test myself.
answers.says: Describes an incident in a system they operated, with a timeline and numbers (time from detection, time to recovery, number of affected cases). Explains, in their own words, what they looked at to triage the cause and the recovery decisions (including who they told and when), and can describe the postmortem's preventive measures and whether they actually worked afterward. If their own mistake caused it, they can describe, matter-of-factly, how they shared that without hiding it.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: Yes, and I'll be honest about it rather than give the tidy answer. During the state-machine incident I just described, I deployed the guard-condition fix myself about ninety minutes in, without waiting for a second reviewer, because claims were actively bypassing fraud review while I waited. I posted in the incident channel right before deploying, not after, saying I was skipping review given active harm, and I logged the diff afterward for the team to review once things were calm. Looking back, I think I could have gotten a one-line ack from anyone online in under two minutes before pushing rather than announcing and going -- the situation didn't actually require skipping that check, just doing it fast, and I've tried to hold myself to a stricter bar since. It's the one time I've done it, and I don't think it was as necessary as it felt in the moment.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: On sharing a mistake: I once shipped a change to claim-amount rounding that was subtly wrong for a specific currency path, and I found it myself two days later while checking something unrelated. I posted about it in our team channel that same afternoon, tagged my manager, and we quantified the impact -- 14 claims, all under $3 difference -- before I'd been asked anything. On-call: I've carried our claims-platform rotation for four years, one week in five, and it's genuinely part of how I think about the job, not separate from it. I also mentor one junior engineer who joined last year, mostly through pairing on incident write-ups, since I think learning to reason about an incident calmly is as much the job as writing the original code.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

fit.says: The candidate is broadly aligned with most of the working principles, but shows a conditional attitude in some areas — for example, saying something to the effect of ‘in an emergency, you should fix it first even if it means skipping the procedure,’ without committing to announcing and recording that skip, or not speaking positively about on-call or support work. They could work here, but some coaching would be needed to bring them fully in line with the principles.
